name: Flipkart
summary: Flipkart's engineering interviews are known for a machine coding round, where candidates commonly report building a small working system in a set time, alongside problem-solving and, for experienced roles, system design. Its careers site says interviewers' feedback goes to an independent hiring committee, and it publishes five values: Audacity, Bias for Action, Customer First, Integrity and Inclusion.
rounds: Machine coding round (build a small working system in 90–120 minutes)

questions.text: Walk me through how you'd design a simple parking-lot or snake-and-ladder system in code.
covers: The main classes and what each is responsible for, from the requirements
A working version first, then how a new rule (vehicle type, board size) fits without rewrites
Edge cases and how you'd test them, such as a full lot or a snake at the last square

questions.text: Tell me about a time you owned a problem end to end.
covers: Why it was yours to own, and what would have happened if you hadn't
The steps you took yourself, from finding the cause to shipping the fix
The result, and what you set up so it stayed fixed

questions.text: How would you design the cart and checkout flow for a big sale day?
covers: Clarifying the load: peak orders per second and the few hot products everyone wants
Reserving stock at checkout without overselling, and releasing it if payment fails
Keeping the rest of the site up: caching, queues, rate limits and graceful fallbacks

questions.text: Tell me about the boldest bet you've made on a project. What happened?
covers: What made it bold: the risk, and what the safe option was
How you made the case and limited the downside
The outcome, including what you learned if it didn't work

questions.text: Describe a time you moved fast to fix something urgent for customers. How did you avoid making it worse?
covers: Who was affected and why waiting wasn't an option
The quick fix and the safety checks around it, such as a flag or a rollback plan
The proper fix you made afterwards

questions.text: Tell me about a time you pushed back on a shortcut because it wasn't right for customers or sellers.
covers: The shortcut, and who it would have hurt
How you raised it and what you offered instead
What was decided, and how you kept your word on the alternative

questions.text: Tell me about a risk you took that didn't work out. What did you take from it?
covers: Why the risk seemed worth taking at the time
How you found out it wasn't working, and how quickly you stopped or changed course
What you'd do the same and what you'd do differently

questions.text: How would you design a flash sale where a limited stock of a popular phone goes on sale at noon?
covers: Stock reservation that can't oversell: atomic counters or holds that expire
Absorbing the noon spike: a waiting queue, cached product pages and rate limits
Fairness and bots, and what shoppers see once stock runs out

questions.text: Explain the SOLID principles with an example from code you've written. Which one do you find hardest to follow?
covers: Each principle in a sentence, tied to a class you actually wrote
How following them made the code easier to extend or test
An honest example of where you broke one and why

questions.text: How would you design product search with filters such as brand, price and rating for a very large catalogue?
covers: A search index with facets for filters, and how it's kept in sync with the catalogue
Ranking: relevance, availability, price and popularity
Spelling mistakes and mixed-language queries, plus speed and caching

questions.text: Delivery dates shown on product pages are wrong for some pin codes. How would you investigate?
covers: Narrowing it down: which pin codes, sellers or warehouses, and since when
Checking each input: serviceability data, warehouse stock, courier timelines
The fix, and a check or alert that would catch it next time

questions.text: How would you improve how many first-time shoppers from smaller towns complete their first order on the app?
covers: Finding where they drop off in the funnel before proposing fixes
Likely barriers: trust, language, payment options such as cash on delivery
An experiment, with first-order conversion as the goal and returns as a guardrail

questions.text: Why Flipkart? Which of its values do you connect with most, and when have you shown it?
covers: A reason tied to the team, product or customers, not only the brand
One value, named once, with a short example
Why that way of working suits you

questions.text: What would you change about the Flipkart app, and how would you know your change worked?
covers: A specific screen or flow, and the customer problem with it
The change you'd make and what you'd leave out
The metric that would tell you it worked

tips: Practise machine coding: working code first, then clean classes and tests.
Talk about scale: Big Billion Days traffic is a favourite topic.
Flipkart's hiring page invites you to ask your recruiter how many rounds to expect; ask what each one covers so you can prepare.
Flipkart says each interviewer's feedback goes to an independent hiring committee, so give every round your full effort, including the last one.
Flipkart says it celebrates its biggest risk that didn't work out each year (its Chandrayaan Award), so have an honest failure story ready.
Its hiring page says you can have only one application under consideration at a time, so choose the role that fits you best.
